title: Register early forwarding selects
motivation:
The baseline timing report shows the critical path beginning at the MEM/WB
destination register, passing through the forwarding unit, then through the
EX operand muxes and ALU before reaching the next state. That means a
same-cycle forwarding comparison is controlling the ALU input path and
directly limiting Fmax, while contributing no useful IPC improvement beyond
ordinary bypass correctness.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Move forwarding hit detection one stage earlier and latch the selected
bypass source with the ID/EX payload. For an instruction being decoded,
compare its rs1/rs2 against the producer currently in ID/EX, which will be
EX/MEM when the consumer executes, and against the producer currently in
EX/MEM, which will be MEM/WB when the consumer executes. The EX stage then
uses registered forwarding selects, removing the rd comparator and priority
chain from the forwarding-to-ALU critical path. Load-use bubbling and dmem
stalls keep the same semantics by holding or clearing the latched selects
with the rest of ID/EX.

title: Move RV32M onto a held multi-cycle execute unit
motivation:
The current vendor timing path starts in pipeline state, flows through the
forwarding network into EX, crosses the monolithic ALU, and ends near the
memory-side outputs. Because the ALU contains fully combinational multiply,
divide, and remainder hardware, every simple ADD, branch compare, and address
calculation pays for deep RV32M arithmetic in the timed EX cone even when the
instruction is not an M-extension op.

address path should retime to a much higher Fmax, improving the fitness product.

title: Static BTFN fetch predictor
motivation:
The current pipeline fetches sequentially and resolves every taken branch or
jump in EX, forcing wrong-path instructions to be flushed. CoreMark contains
tight loops and frequent unconditional JAL control flow, so the always-not-
taken policy pays the redirect penalty repeatedly on hot backward branches
and calls even when their targets are immediate constants available at fetch.

hypothesis.hypothesis:

recognize conditional branches with negative B-immediates and unconditional

correction behavior. The added IF decode/adder is small compared with the
current ALU/forwarding critical path, so the expected gain is primarily IPC.

title: Split ID/EX bubble control from payload data
motivation:
After the RV32M split, the vendor timing path moved to a much smaller
regfile-to-ID/EX path that loops through execute redirect, fetch flush,
hazard control, and back into the ID/EX register enables. The data payload
bits of the ID/EX register do not need to be cleared on redirect, load-use,
or mul/div busy bubbles as long as the valid bit and side-effecting control
fields are bubbled. Removing those fast-changing bubble conditions from the
wide rs1/rs2/pc/instr/immediate payload muxes should shorten the new critical
cone without changing instruction retirement semantics.

motivation:
After moving RV32M out of the common execute cone, the reported worst path is
no longer arithmetic-heavy. It now loops from decoded operand state through
EX redirect/branch logic, IF flush handling, the hazard unit, and back into
the ID/EX register controls. That same-cycle squash feedback costs Fmax on
every instruction even though it only matters when a branch or jump redirects.

title: Tiny EX-trained BTB predictor
motivation:
The current core still fetches sequentially until EX resolves taken branches
and jumps, so hot CoreMark loop backedges and direct jumps pay repeated
wrong-path bubbles. The previous static BTFN attempt showed that doing
immediate decode and target addition in IF is too expensive for this FPGA
timing point, so the next predictor should learn already-resolved targets
instead of recomputing them on the fetch path.

title: Bypass ALU mux for memory addresses
motivation:
After the RV32M split and the ID/EX bubble cleanup, the reported worst path
is a much smaller execute cone that still runs through u_ex/u_alu before
reaching memory-side timing endpoints. Loads and stores only need rs1+imm for
the data-memory address, but today that address is carried in the same
generic alu_result field used by shifts, compares, logical ops, AUIPC, and
jump link results. That makes every memory access pay for the full ALU result
selection even though the operation is always an add.

title: Decoupled two-entry instruction fetch queue
motivation:
The best current core is now limited by a modest execute path, while random
instruction-memory stalls still inject bubbles whenever io_imemReady is low.
CoreMark also has dmem stalls, load-use bubbles, redirects, and multi-cycle
RV32M operations that stop decode but do not inherently need to stop the
instruction bus from fetching future sequential instructions. A small
front-end queue should convert some of those backend stall cycles into useful
prefetch slack, improving iterations per cycle without putting branch
prediction, target adders, or tag lookups on the PC loop.

A narrower structural target is the branch comparator topology itself: conditional branches currently use the same post-forward 32-bit operand muxes as the ALU, so forwarding select logic sits in front of the branch compare and redirect decision.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Restructure EX branch resolution as a small parallel compare matrix. For conditional branches, compute compare results for the possible rs1/rs2 forwarding sources in parallel, then use the existing forwarding selects only to choose the one-bit branch result. The ordinary ALU operand muxes remain for arithmetic, load/store address, JALR target, and RVFI operand reporting, but the timing-critical branch-taken-to-IF redirect path no longer needs to traverse two wide 3-way operand muxes before the equality or magnitude comparator.

This keeps the current metadata-free direct-JAL decode redirect, the two-entry IF FIFO, the single-cycle conditional branch resolution point, and all RVFI ordering semantics. It spends LUTs on duplicated branch compare logic rather than adding pipeline latency or front-end prediction state, aiming for a pure Fmax gain on the current u_id/u_ex/u_if critical cone with unchanged CoreMark cycles.

title: Metadata-free backward branch predictor
motivation:
Prior predictor attempts show that the front end cannot afford tables,
tags, loop counters, return stacks, or carried predicted-next-PC metadata.
The current champion succeeds only for aligned direct JAL because decode
redirects with no repair metadata and EX can suppress the duplicate redirect
deterministically. CoreMark still contains hot backward conditional branches,
and the existing decode stage already computes pc+imm for the direct-JAL
redirect path, so there is a narrow opportunity to predict loop backedges
without adding another target adder or predictor state.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Extend the current metadata-free decode redirect from aligned direct JAL to
aligned negative-offset conditional branches using a static backward-taken,
forward-not-taken policy. In ID, when an accepted valid conditional branch
has a negative B-immediate and the existing pc+imm target is word-aligned,
redirect the IF queue to that target just like the current direct-JAL path.

Do not add a BTB, tag compare, counter, target cache, or predicted-next-PC
field. EX can recompute the same static policy from the carried branch
immediate and resolved target: suppress the duplicate redirect when the
backward branch is actually taken, repair to pc+4 when the predicted
backward branch falls through, and keep the current taken redirect for
forward branches. This should harvest CoreMark loop-back IPC while avoiding
the specific metadata and compare costs that sank the last-taken branch
predictor.

title: Valid-qualified bubble control
motivation:
The best micro-optimizations on this core removed high-fanout bubble and
redirect control from wide datapath flops without adding new predictor or
target-address logic. The current ID/EX stage still drives every decoded
control bit through a bubble mux, so EX redirect, load-use, empty-IF, and
mul/div busy conditions fan into the full ctrl_t register even though an
invalid pipeline entry should be made harmless by its valid bit.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Treat the pipeline valid bits as the sole architectural side-effect
qualifiers for bubbles. Latch decoded ctrl_t normally whenever ID/EX is not
held, even on bubble cycles, and clear only ID/EX.valid. Then audit the few
places that currently assume bubbled control bits are zero: qualify load-use
detection with id_ex.valid, qualify EX/MEM memory-stall detection with
ex_mem.valid, and gate dmem read/write/misalignment behavior with the
EX/MEM valid bit.

This should remove the bubble/redirect signal from the decoded-control
register fanout and shrink the fragile ID-to-EX-to-IF control cone while
preserving cycle count, forwarding priority, direct-JAL decode redirects,
memory side effects, and RVFI retirement semantics. The change is deliberately
smaller than prior failed predictor and operand-isolation attempts: it deletes
bubble muxing from existing control flops and adds only local valid guards
where invalid entries could otherwise affect hazards or memory ports.

title: Release EX on RV32M result cycle
motivation:
The current best core is limited by a fragile IF/ID/EX redirect path, and
recent predictor, cache, branch-matrix, and extra-front-end-state attempts
have mostly traded CoreMark IPC for worse Fmax. The earlier structural
RV32M split was the largest win because it kept multiply/divide hardware
out of the common ALU path, but the held EX handshake still treats the
result-return cycle as busy. That conservatively inserts one extra decode
bubble after every completed MUL/DIV/REM even though the completed result
can be written into EX/MEM at the same clock edge.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Refactor the multi-cycle execute handshake so the RV32M unit has distinct
"accepting a new M op", "waiting for the result", and "result will be
emitted this cycle" states. When muldiv_done is high and there is no dmem
stall, EX should capture the saved M-operation payload and result into
EX/MEM while reporting ready to hazard control, allowing decode to accept
the next instruction in that same cycle. The next instruction then reaches
EX one cycle earlier, while forwarding from the just-completed M result
still works through the normal EX/MEM and MEM/WB paths.

This keeps the registered multiplier/divider off the normal ALU timing
cone, does not add prediction metadata or fetch-side target logic, and
preserves in-order single retirement. CoreMark's matrix and list code
execute enough RV32M operations that removing one structural bubble per M
completion should improve cycles without materially changing Fmax; the
added logic is a narrow ready/done distinction local to ex_stage and the
hazard unit.

title: Opcode-fast direct-JAL predictor
motivation:
Prior predictor attempts show that this core cannot afford front-end tables,
tags, return stacks, loop counters, or carried prediction metadata. The only
predictor-like change that improved the champion is the current metadata-free
aligned direct-JAL decode redirect. The remaining avoidable cost is that the
redirect qualifier waits on the general decoder outputs even though every
instruction with opcode 1101111 is a legal direct JAL in RV32I.
